analysis.one_liner: Requires expanded offshore oil and gas leasing and uses the revenue to fund roads and water infrastructure.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and its subcommittees in March 2015 and never received a vote or any further action before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced the Interior Department to open large parts of the outer Continental Shelf — including waters off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California — to oil and gas leasing, with a production target of 3 million more barrels of oil per day by 2033. It would then borrow up to $25 billion a year against the expected leasing revenues and route the money to highways and water systems. It also would have given coastal states a 37.5% share of new offshore revenues, abolished the Minerals Management Service in favor of new leasing and safety offices, and added ethics and drug-testing requirements for officials who deal with energy companies. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, oil and gas companies would gain access to mandated lease sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California with a required share of the most promising acreage. Companies that build highways and water systems would gain a new stream of bond-funded contracts. Coastal state governments within 200 miles of new leases would receive 37.5% of leasing revenues for any state purpose. Motorists and water users would benefit if the infrastructure spending actually materialized.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated funding stream for highways, transit, and water infrastructure by allowing Treasury to issue up to $25 billion per year (2015-2020) in infrastructure revenue bonds, with 95% of proceeds going to the Highway Trust Fund and 5% to state wastewater and drinking water funds [S2][S3].
Gives coastal states within 200 miles of new offshore leases 37.5% of the resulting federal leasing revenues, phased in from 12.5% to 37.5%, usable for any state purpose [S2].

Directs federal oil and gas production toward a stated goal of 3 million more barrels of oil and 10 billion more cubic feet of natural gas per day by 2033, framed as reducing reliance on foreign energy [S2][S3].

Imposes modest ethics and safety measures on the offshore program: annual ethics certification and random drug testing for Interior officials who deal with energy companies, an inspector training academy, a safety advisory board, and inspection fees on operators to fund the inspection program [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the cost would fall on coastal environments and communities near new lease sales, on taxpayers if offshore revenues fall short of the debt issued against them, and on future generations bearing the oil-spill and climate risks of expanded offshore drilling. The federal treasury would also lose 37.5% of new leasing revenues to coastal states.

drawbacks.text: The bill would make offshore leasing effectively mandatory: the Interior Secretary would be required to offer at least 50% of the unleased acreage in the most oil- and gas-rich offshore planning areas, and to hold new lease sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California, including areas that have been off-limits for decades.

The required environmental review would be narrowed: the Secretary would not have to analyze any non-leasing alternative or more than one alternative leasing proposal under the National Environmental Policy Act [S2][S3].

The infrastructure funding is debt-financed: the Treasury could issue up to $25 billion per year of bonds from 2015 through 2020, repaid only from offshore leasing revenues, with no federal guarantee — so if leasing revenues fall short, the infrastructure money is at risk [S3].
The bill would redirect 37.5% of new offshore energy revenues to coastal states rather than to the federal treasury that funds programs for everyone [S2][S3].
The bill would bar Interior Department employees who conduct offshore permitting and inspections from participating in or asserting the right to strike [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The infrastructure funding idea is real — highway and water systems need money — but the bill would pay for it by mandating offshore oil and gas leasing in areas that are currently off-limits, including off California, Virginia, and South Carolina, and by narrowing the environmental review of those sales [S2][S3]. The costs — expanded drilling off sensitive coasts, higher future oil-spill and climate risk, and 37.5% of new federal energy revenues permanently diverted from the Treasury to nearby states — would outweigh the infrastructure benefit, which could be funded through less consequential means. The safety and ethics provisions are modest improvements but would not offset the mandatory-leasing core.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and several subcommittees in March 2015, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 4, 2015, by Rep. Steve Stivers with one Democratic cosponsor, Rep. Cedric Richmond [S1][S5].

It was referred to four committees — Natural Resources, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce — and then to subcommittees on Highways and Transit, Water Resources and Environment, Energy and Power, and Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and no further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore drilling opponents and coastal communities in states like California, Virginia, and South Carolina that the bill would have opened to drilling are better off that it died; the oil and gas industry gains nothing new, though existing federal offshore leasing continues under separate law.

for.name: Rep. Steve Stivers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 4, 2015, which would have mandated expanded offshore oil and gas leasing and used the revenues for infrastructure bonds.

for.name: Rep. Cedric Richmond
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor in the House.

for.name: House Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Ways and Means Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2015 and took no further action on it — no markup, no report, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sole sponsor was a Republican and its sole cosponsor was a Democrat, but with only two members involved and no votes or committee action, the partisan shape of any potential opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would require the Interior Secretary to offer for lease at least half the unleased acreage in the richest offshore planning areas and to hold mandated sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California, with only one leasing alternative analyzed in the environmental review. It would also cap inspection fees at set amounts through 2024. Source: [S3].
A dedicated stream of up to $25 billion a year in bond proceeds would flow 95% to the Highway Trust Fund, creating guaranteed demand for road and transit construction. Source: [S3].

States within 200 miles of new offshore leases would receive 37.5% of the leasing revenues for any state purpose — a large new unrestricted revenue source, though it comes from expanding drilling off their coasts. Source: [S2].

The bill would abolish the Minerals Management Service and rebuild it as separate leasing, safety, and revenue offices with a training academy, mandatory ethics certification, drug testing, and a no-strike rule for inspectors — a reorganization in the same direction as the post-Deepwater Horizon restructuring that already happened administratively. Source: [S2].
